content.text: CCNA 200-301 STUDY MANUAL
Chapter 11
Network Address Translation (NAT)

This document replaces Chapter 11 of Todd Lammle, CCNA Certification Study Guide, Volume 2 (2020), book pages 319 to 336. It follows the book's order and numbering, keeps the book's learning objective, and marks every place where it adds to, corrects, or could not verify the book. It covers static NAT, dynamic NAT, and PAT (overload), with verification, troubleshooting, labs, and review questions.
| Item | Detail |
| Book pages | 319 to 336 (PDF pages 377 to 394; the +58 page offset was re-checked and still holds). PDF page 394 is blank. Chapter 12 starts on book page 337. |

| Tracker rows | Chapter 11 - Network Address Translation (NAT); 11.1, 11.2, 11.3, 11.4, 11.4.1, 11.4.2, 11.4.3, 11.4.4, 11.5. Seq numbers were not read: there was no Notion tool in this chat. CHECK |
| Suggested time | About 3 to 4 hours including the labs. This is a suggestion, not a measured need. |
| Exam versions | Book: v1.0 objective 4.1. v1.1 (retires 2 Feb 2027): 4.1. v2.0 (first exam 3 Feb 2027): 4.3 Configure NAT/PAT on IOS XE routers. |
| Status of your knowledge | Not assessed |
| Tag | Meaning |
| BOOK | Taken from the book. |
| UPDATED | The book is outdated, wrong, or unclear. The text says what changed and why. |
| ADDED | Extra material that is not in the book chapter. |
| CHECK | Not verified. Commands and outputs marked this way were NOT run on real Cisco equipment. |
WHAT THE BOOK SAYS
Learning objective (from the book). One exam objective is listed for this chapter: 4.1 Configure and verify inside source NAT using static and pools.

Chapter goal. Hosts on an inside corporate network use RFC 1918 private addresses. They need Internet access, so you configure NAT translations on the border router. Access lists from Chapter 10 are used inside the NAT commands. BOOK
VERIFY

Verification note. Every address, mask, wildcard, and pool size in this document was calculated with a Python ipaddress script and compared with the block-size method. The script is in the build folder as ch11_verify.py.

No command in this document was run on real Cisco equipment. Command outputs are illustrative and tagged CHECK . Facts that could have changed were checked against Cisco, IANA, and other sources; the Sources table at the end says which were official.
Where this chapter fits in the exam
| Section | v1.1 | v2.0 | Priority |
| 11.1 When Do We Use NAT? | 4.1 (background) | 4.3 (background); 1.3 public and private addressing | Medium |
| 11.2 Types of NAT | 4.1 (static and pools) | 4.3 NAT/PAT | High |
| 11.3 NAT Names | 4.1 | 4.3 | High |
| 11.4 How NAT Works | 4.1 | 4.3 | High |
| 11.4.1 Static NAT | 4.1 static | 4.3 | High |
| 11.4.2 Dynamic NAT | 4.1 pools | 4.3 | High |
| 11.4.3 PAT (overload) | 4.1 (pool with overload) | 4.3 names PAT directly | High |
| 11.4.4 Verification | 4.1 verify | 4.3; 2.4 show commands for troubleshooting | High |
| 11.5 Testing and Troubleshooting | 4.1 verify | 2.4; 4.3 | High |
| ACLs used by NAT (Chapter 10) | ACL objective (number not re-checked) | 4.6 IPv4 ACLs | Related |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE
v2.0 says "NAT/PAT on IOS XE routers", so use IOS XE syntax. The core commands in this chapter are the same. CHECK on real IOS XE.

The v1.1 wording says "static and pools" and never says PAT. A pool with overload is PAT, and it is the form used in almost every real network, so learn it fully. Cisco also says related topics may appear on any exam. v1.1 wording is from a secondary source because Cisco's own v1.1 PDF could not be opened. CHECK

Answer these five questions before you read the chapter. Write your answer and one confidence tag: K (I know it), U (I think I understand), G (I am guessing). Answers are in Answer Key A at the end. Do not look yet. This is how you find out what you really know. The tracker stays Not assessed until you show understanding.
| # | Question | Your answer | K / U / G |
| 1 | What problem was NAT first made to slow down? |  |  |
| 3 | What does the keyword overload do in a NAT command? |  |  |
| 4 | In show ip nat translations, which column shows the private address of the inside host? |  |  |
| 5 | Which two interface commands must exist for NAT to translate anything? |  |  |
Book page 320.

The idea in plain words. Offices and homes use private IPv4 addresses. Routers on the Internet do not forward packets with private source addresses. NAT fixes this: the border router swaps the private source address for a public one on the way out, and swaps it back on the way in. The router remembers each swap in a NAT table. BOOK

The book says NAT was first meant to slow the use of IPv4 addresses, like CIDR did. It later turned out to help with mergers (two companies with the same private addresses), a change of ISP without renumbering the inside network, server load sharing, and virtual servers. BOOK
The private ranges (RFC 1918)
| Range | First to last address | Note |
The book mentions RFC 1918 here but does not list the ranges in this chapter. ADDED The ranges are general knowledge; the 172.16.0.0/12 end address was confirmed with the script.
Where NAT goes

NAT is configured on the border router between the inside LAN (private addresses) and the ISP (public addresses). The LAN-facing interface is the inside interface. The ISP-facing interface is the outside interface (Figure 11.1). BOOK
Advantages and disadvantages (Table 11.1)
| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| Conserves legally registered (public) addresses | Translation adds switching path delay |
| Remedies address overlap, for example after a merger | Loss of end-to-end IP traceability |
| More flexibility when connecting to the Internet | Some applications do not work with NAT |
| No renumbering when the network changes (for example a new ISP) | Complicates tunnels such as IPsec, because NAT changes header values |
EXAM CRITICAL

Know the four advantages and four disadvantages. Book review questions 1 and 2 ask for them as "choose three". Read the wording carefully: "conserves addresses" and "remedies overlap" are advantages; "delay", "loss of traceability", and "some apps break" are disadvantages.
MEMORY TIP
Private second octet for 172: 16 to 31. If it is 15 or 32, the address is public.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The book says NAT/PAT is why IPv4 "only recently" ran out, and that without it addresses would have run out "more than a decade ago". This is the author's opinion and the wording is dated. I did not verify when each regional registry ran out of addresses. CHECK
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)
NAT is not a firewall. It hides inside addresses as a side effect, but you still need ACLs or a firewall for security. ADDED General knowledge, not verified in this session.
Some ISPs also translate customers a second time (carrier-grade NAT). This is not on the exam. ADDED CHECK
Quick check: 11.1
Q1. Which one is an advantage of NAT?
A. Loss of end-to-end IP traceability
B. It remedies address overlap when networks merge
C. Translation adds switching path delay
D. Some applications will not work
Answer: B - the other three are the disadvantages in Table 11.1.
Q2. Where is NAT usually configured?
Answer: On the border router between the inside LAN and the ISP - the LAN side is inside and the ISP side is outside.
Q3. Is 172.32.5.1 a private address?
Q4. Name two situations where NAT helps besides saving addresses.
Answer: Any two of: merging networks with overlapping addresses; changing ISP without renumbering; server load sharing; virtual servers - from the book's list on pages 320 to 321.
Book page 322.
The idea in plain words. The three types differ in how the router picks the public address.
| Type | Mapping | Uses port numbers? | Public addresses needed | Typical use |
| Static NAT | One-to-one, fixed by you | No | One per inside host | A server that must always be reachable at the same public address |
| Dynamic NAT | Many-to-many, taken from a pool | No | At least one per host that is online at the same time | Rare today |
| Overloading (PAT) | Many-to-one (or many-to-few) | Yes, the source port tells hosts apart | One, or a few | Almost every home and office |
PAT (Port Address Translation) is also called NAT overload. It is dynamic NAT plus the keyword overload. It is not a fourth type. BOOK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Book inconsistency. The heading on page 322 says overloading is "one-to-many", but the next line says "many-to-one". The correct picture is many inside hosts share one public address (many-to-one). UPDATED
The book says PAT lets "about 65,000 hosts" share one address. That is a theory number (the port field has 16 bits). The real limit is lower and depends on the platform and traffic. CHECK
EXAM CRITICAL
Book review question 8: the three NAT methods are static, dynamic, and overload. "IP NAT pool" is a command, and "NAT double-translation" is not a method.
COMMON MISTAKE
Do not think dynamic NAT can serve more hosts than the pool has addresses. With a 2-address pool and no overload, a third host cannot get out until an entry is cleared or times out.
Quick check: 11.2
Q1. Which NAT type uses source port numbers to tell inside hosts apart?
Answer: Overloading (PAT) - the same public address is shared and ports keep the conversations separate.
Q2. You have 5 internal servers that each need their own fixed public address. Which type, and how many public addresses?
Answer: Static NAT, 5 addresses - static is one-to-one.
Q3. True or false: PAT is a separate command from NAT.
Answer: False - it is dynamic NAT with the overload keyword.
Book pages 322 to 323.
The idea in plain words. NAT uses four names for addresses. Two simple rules make them easy:
- Inside / Outside says where the host is: on the inside network, or on the outside network.
- Local / Global says whose point of view: Local = how the inside network sees the address. Global = how the outside network sees the address.
| Name | Where is the host? | Seen from | Example (PAT, book Figure 11.3) |
| Inside local | Inside | The inside network | 10.1.1.1:1026 (private address) |
| Inside global | Inside | The outside network | 170.168.2.1:1026 (public address after translation) |
| Outside local | Outside | The inside network | 63.40.7.3:80 (the server, as the inside network sees it) |
| Outside global | Outside | The outside network | 63.40.7.3:80 (the server, its real address) |

In normal Internet access nobody translates the destination, so outside local = outside global (the server's real address). They only differ if you use ip nat outside source, which is not on the exam. UPDATED
What the book says versus what Cisco says
| Item | Book (pages 322 to 323) | Cisco definition | Verdict |

| Local / global | Global = address used after translation. Local = address used before translation. | Local = seen on the inside network. Global = seen on the outside network. | Book is a shortcut. It works for inside addresses only. UPDATED |
| Inside local | Inside host address before translation, usually RFC 1918 | Same | Correct BOOK |
| Inside global | Inside host address after translation, the real Internet address | Same | Correct BOOK |

| Outside local | Usually the address of the router interface connected to the ISP | Address of an outside host as it appears to the inside network | Book is wrong. The ISP-facing router interface is not the outside local address. UPDATED |
| Outside global | Address of the outside destination host | Same | Correct BOOK |
EXAM CRITICAL

In show ip nat translations the columns are in this order: Pro, Inside global, Inside local, Outside local, Outside global. The global address of the inside host is listed before the local one. This order is a classic trap.
Assessment-test question 30 and the Chapter 11 questions use the same terms: the inside host's address after translation is the inside global.
MEMORY TIP
Local = LAN view. Global = Internet view. Inside = my side. Outside = their side.
WHY THIS MATTERS
These four names are the column headings in the main NAT verification command. If you mix them up, you will read the table backwards and troubleshoot the wrong thing.
Quick check: 11.3
Q1. Which name is the private address of the inside host before translation?
Answer: Inside local - inside host, seen from the inside network.
Q2. After PAT, the public address used for that host is called?
Answer: Inside global - inside host, seen from the outside network.
Q3. When a PC browses a web server on the Internet with normal PAT, how do outside local and outside global compare?
Answer: They are the same address - the destination address is not translated.
Q4. Which address column is listed first in show ip nat translations, inside local or inside global?
Answer: Inside global - the column order is Inside global, Inside local, Outside local, Outside global.
Book pages 323 to 325.
Basic translation (book Figure 11.2)
Three inside hosts (10.1.1.1, 10.1.1.2, 10.1.1.3) share a pool. Each one gets its own inside global address, and the router writes each pair in the NAT table:
| Inside local | Inside global |
Step by step. BOOK
- Host 10.1.1.1 (inside local) sends a packet to Host B, 63.40.7.3. The NAT router is its default gateway.
- The packet arrives on the router's inside interface. The router finds the route to the destination out of the outside interface.
- The router rewrites the source address to an inside global address (170.168.2.2) and records the pair in the NAT table.
- Host B replies to 170.168.2.2.
- The reply arrives on the outside interface. The router looks in the NAT table, rewrites the destination back to 10.1.1.1, and forwards it into the LAN.
- The entry stays in the table until its timer runs out (see 11.5).
Overloading, or PAT (book Figure 11.3)
With PAT every inside host is translated to one address. The router tells the hosts apart by their source port:
| Inside local | Inside global |

In the book's example, host 10.1.1.1 browses a web server. The packet leaves with destination port 80. The server answers to port 1026, and the router uses port 1026 to find the right inside host. Ports work at the Transport layer, which is how many hosts can share one IP address. BOOK
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Order of operations (Cisco). Inside to outside: the router routes first, then translates. Outside to inside: the router translates first, then routes. The NAT router must also have a valid route for the inside local address. This is why many NAT problems are really routing problems. ADDED Source: Cisco NAT order-of-operations document (official).
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Book wording on page 324 to 325: "If we had to use real global IP addresses to identify the source hosts, that's called static NAT." One real address per host is static NAT, or dynamic NAT without overload. PAT is what uses ports to identify hosts. UPDATED
WHY THIS MATTERS
PAT is why one broadband router can serve a whole house with one public address. It is the most used form of NAT.
Quick check: 11.4
Q1. On the way out, which part of the packet does NAT change?
Answer: The source address (and the source port with PAT) - the destination is not changed.
Q2. What does the router do first with a packet that arrives on the outside interface for an inside host: route it or translate it?
Answer: Translate it, then route it - Cisco's order of operations for outside-to-inside traffic.
Q3. In PAT, what lets the router send a reply to the correct inside host?
Answer: The port number in the NAT table - all hosts share one inside global IP address.
11.4.1 Static NAT Configuration
Book page 325. Static NAT maps one inside local address to one inside global address, and you type the mapping yourself.
Book example, static NAT BOOK
ip nat inside source static 10.1.1.1 170.46.2.2
interface Ethernet0
ip nat inside
interface Serial0
ip nat outside
- ip nat inside source static: translate the source address of packets that come from the inside, using a fixed mapping.
- 10.1.1.1: the inside local address (the private host).
- 170.46.2.2: the inside global address (the public address). On page 325 the book calls this the "outside global" address. That is a mistake. UPDATED
- ip nat inside on Ethernet0: this interface faces the private LAN.
- ip nat outside on Serial0: this interface faces the ISP.
Illustrative output CHECK
Router# show ip nat translations
Pro Inside global Inside local Outside local Outside global
A static entry appears with --- in the port columns, and it is there even when no traffic is flowing, because you configured it.
COMMON MISTAKE

On page 325 the book says ip nat outside source makes the outside interface "the source or starting point of the translation". That is not what it does. ip nat outside source translates the address of a host that is outside. It is not on the exam. For this exam, always read inside source as "translate the source address of packets from the inside". UPDATED
EXAM CRITICAL

Static NAT needs one public address per inside host. It works in both directions, so an outside host can start a connection to the inside global address (if ACLs allow it). ADDED General knowledge. One of the most common exam problems is inside and outside set on the wrong interfaces (book, page 326).
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Static NAT can also map one port only (port forwarding), for example ip nat inside source static tcp 192.168.10.100 80 203.0.113.2 80. It is not in the book and not in the objective wording. ADDED CHECK
Quick check: 11.4.1
Q1. In ip nat inside source static 10.1.1.1 170.46.2.2, which address is the inside local?
Answer: 10.1.1.1 - the first address is the private host, the second is the public address.
Q2. Name the two interface commands that must go with a NAT configuration.
Answer: ip nat inside and ip nat outside - NAT only translates between an inside and an outside interface.
Q3. Does a static NAT entry appear in the table before any traffic is sent?
Answer: Yes - it is configured, not created by traffic.
11.4.2 Dynamic NAT Configuration
Book pages 325 to 326. Dynamic NAT gives inside hosts a public address from a pool, first come first served. No port numbers are used, so each active inside host needs its own public address.
Book example, dynamic NAT BOOK
ip nat inside source list 1 pool todd
interface Ethernet0
ip nat inside
interface Serial0
ip nat outside
access-list 1 permit 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255
- ip nat pool todd: creates a pool named todd. The name is case sensitive.
- 170.168.2.3 170.168.2.254: the first and last public address in the pool. That is 252 addresses (checked by script).
- netmask 255.255.255.0: the mask that tells IOS the whole range is in one subnet. prefix-length 24 does the same thing. (You cannot use prefix-length on an interface IP address.)
- ip nat inside source list 1 pool todd: translate the source addresses matched by ACL 1, using pool todd. The pool name must match exactly.

- access-list 1 permit 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255: matches inside hosts 10.1.1.0 to 10.1.1.255. Here the ACL only selects which traffic to translate (the book calls it "interesting traffic"). It is not a security filter.
EXAM CRITICAL

When troubleshooting a pool: check that the pool has enough addresses for all hosts online at the same time, and that the pool name matches exactly on both lines. Case matters. If the names differ, the pool does not work. BOOK
The book also says IOS will not let you change or delete a pool while any of its addresses are mapped in the NAT table. Clear the entries first. BOOK CHECK on hardware.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)
Cisco's configuration guide says NAT does not support permit ip any any in the access list used with a NAT command. Use the specific inside network instead. ADDED Official Cisco source.
A deny line in the NAT ACL means "do not translate this traffic". It does not drop the traffic. ADDED CHECK Secondary source only.
MEMORY TIP
ACL wildcard mask = 255 minus each mask octet. For a /24 (255.255.255.0) the wildcard is 0.0.0.255. This is the same skill you used in Chapter 10.
Quick check: 11.4.2
Q1. In dynamic NAT, what is the job of the access list?
Answer: To select which inside addresses are translated - it is not a security filter here.
Q2. Your config has ip nat pool Corp ... and ip nat inside source list 1 pool corp. Will it work?
Answer: No - pool names are case sensitive, so Corp and corp are different pools.
Q3. The pool has 2 addresses and no overload. Three inside hosts try to reach the Internet at the same time. What happens to the third?
Answer: It cannot be translated until a pool address is free - dynamic NAT without ports needs one public address per active host. CHECK exact symptom on hardware.
11.4.3 PAT (Overloading) Configuration
Book pages 326 to 327. This is the form used almost everywhere. It is the same as dynamic NAT with two changes: the pool shrinks to one address, and overload is added.
Book example, PAT BOOK
ip nat pool globalnet 170.168.2.1 170.168.2.1 netmask 255.255.255.0
ip nat inside source list 1 pool globalnet overload
interface Ethernet0/0
ip nat inside
interface Serial0/0
ip nat outside
access-list 1 permit 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255
- ip nat pool globalnet 170.168.2.1 170.168.2.1 ...: a pool with only one address. Start and end are the same. Here it is the same address as the outside interface.
- overload: turns dynamic NAT into PAT, so many inside hosts share that one address using different ports.
- You can add more addresses to the pool if one address is not enough for a very large site. BOOK
Two ways to write PAT
| Form | Command | Public address used |
| A. Pool | ip nat inside source list 1 pool NAME overload | The address or addresses in the pool |
| B. Interface | ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1 overload | Whatever IP address the outside interface has right now |
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Form B is common in real networks and is shown in Cisco's own overload example. It follows the interface address if the ISP changes it, so you do not edit a pool. The book mentions it on page 333 only as a one-liner. ADDED
COMMON MISTAKE

On page 333 the book describes the one-line interface form as "use my outside local as my inside global". The correct description is: use the outside interface's own address as the inside global address, and overload it. UPDATED
Quick check: 11.4.3
Q1. Which keyword changes dynamic NAT into PAT?
Answer: overload - it lets many hosts share one inside global address using ports.
Q2. Write the one-line PAT command that uses the outside interface Serial0/0/0 and ACL 1.
Answer: ip nat inside source list 1 interface Serial0/0/0 overload - the interface form needs no pool.
Q3. Besides the NAT command, what else must be configured for the line above to work?
Answer: ACL 1, ip nat inside and ip nat outside on the interfaces - the ACL selects the hosts, the interface commands set the direction.
11.4.4 Simple Verification of NAT
Book page 327.
| Command | What it does | Note |
| show ip nat translations | Lists the active NAT table entries | First command to use |
| show ip nat statistics | Summary: active translations, hits, misses, expired entries, pool details | BOOK page 329 |
| debug ip nat | Shows each translation as it happens | Heavy. Use only briefly in a lab, then undebug all. ADDED |
| clear ip nat translation * | Removes all dynamic entries | Static entries stay. Add a specific entry to clear only that one. |
| show ip nat translations verbose | More detail for each entry | ADDED CHECK |
| show access-lists | Shows whether the NAT ACL matches your hosts | ADDED |
Illustrative output of a dynamic entry after a ping CHECK
R1# show ip nat translations
Pro Inside global Inside local Outside local Outside global
The book says you will usually see many translations from the same host to the same destination. This is normal when there are many connections to one server. BOOK
WARNING
debug ip nat can flood a busy router and make the CLI hard to use. In a real network prefer show commands. Turn debug off with undebug all.
Quick check: 11.4.4
Q1. Which command shows the active NAT entries?
Answer: show ip nat translations - it is the translation table.
Q2. Which command shows hits, misses and expired translations?
Answer: show ip nat statistics - it is the NAT summary.
Q3. Does clear ip nat translation * remove static entries?
Answer: No, only dynamic entries - static entries are configured and stay. CHECK on hardware.
Book pages 328 to 333.
The book's checklist
| Check | How |
| Dynamic pools hold the right scope of addresses | show ip nat statistics; the running config line ip nat pool |
| Pools do not overlap each other | Compare the start and end of each pool |
| Static addresses do not overlap pool addresses | Compare ip nat inside source static lines with the pools |
| ACLs list the correct addresses to translate | show access-lists. None left out, none included by mistake. |
| Inside and outside interfaces are set correctly | show running-config interface ... |
| Routing is correct after translation (the book says this is often the real problem) | show ip route, ping from the router |
Reading the translation table
Output A: no port numbers CHECK
Pro Inside global Inside local Outside local Outside global
Output A is static or dynamic NAT. You cannot tell which one from the table alone, but you can tell it is not PAT, because there are no ports. BOOK
Output B: ports and one shared inside global address CHECK
Pro Inside global Inside local Outside local Outside global
Output B is PAT. The protocol is TCP, there are port numbers, and the inside global address is the same in both lines. BOOK
Limits, statistics, debug, and clearing

- Table size. The book says each mapping uses about 160 bytes of memory, and you can cap the table with ip nat translation max-entries. One secondary source says 160 to 200 bytes and it depends on the platform. Do not memorize the number. CHECK

- Statistics. show ip nat statistics counts active translations, hits (a packet matched an existing mapping), misses (no mapping yet, so the router tries to create one), and expired translations. The book says to add the keyword pool after statistics for pool details. I could not confirm that exact syntax. Pool details normally appear in the show ip nat statistics output itself. CHECK
- Clearing. Clear one entry or all dynamic entries. Use clear ip nat translation * for all dynamic entries. IOS will not change a pool while its addresses are mapped, so clear first. BOOK
Illustrative debug lines CHECK
- s= is the source, d= is the destination. The arrow -> shows the address that was changed.
- The first line is an inside-to-outside packet (source changed). The second is the reply (destination changed back).
- The asterisk in NAT* means the packet was translated in the fast path. The book calls this "fast-switched". CHECK
- The number in brackets is most likely the IP identification value. CHECK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The book's "route once switch many" fast-switching explanation (page 329) describes old cache-based switching. Modern Cisco routers use CEF. The asterisk idea still helps you read debug lines, but do not memorize fast-switching as exam content. UPDATED General knowledge. CHECK
Timeouts

When an entry is created a timer starts. Each packet that uses the entry resets it. When the timer ends the entry is removed, and a dynamic address goes back to the pool. The book gives one default, 86,400 seconds (24 hours), changed with ip nat translation timeout. BOOK
That is only part of the picture. With PAT each protocol has its own timer. ADDED
| Entry type | Default | Command |
| Simple (non-port) entries | 86,400 s (24 h) | ip nat translation timeout seconds |
| TCP port entries | 86,400 s (24 h) | ip nat translation tcp-timeout seconds |
| UDP port entries | 300 s (5 min) | ip nat translation udp-timeout seconds |
| DNS | 60 s | ip nat translation dns-timeout seconds |
| ICMP | 60 s | ip nat translation icmp-timeout seconds |
| TCP SYN / FIN and RST | 60 s | ip nat translation syn-timeout and finrst-timeout |
VERIFY

The timer values come from a Cisco community document (86,400 s for simple and TCP entries, 5 minutes for UDP, 1 minute for DNS) and from a reference book (ICMP, SYN, FIN/RST). Timers can differ by platform and software version. Confirm on your own router. CHECK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The book (page 330) says the outside device's packet destination address in a reply "is known as the inside global address". The idea is right but the sentence is hard to read. A reply packet's destination is the inside global address. After translation it becomes the inside local address. UPDATED
Worked examples from the book (pages 330 to 333)
Example 1 (Figure 11.4): which type?
The book says NAT goes on the corporate border router, as in Figure 11.1, and the design needs dynamic NAT with overload. Then it shows this configuration and asks what type it is:
Book example BOOK
ip nat inside source list 1 pool todd-nat
Answer: dynamic NAT without PAT. The pool holds 11 addresses (checked by script) and there is no overload at the end. BOOK
Example 2 (Figure 11.5): 62 inside hosts, six public addresses
Inside hosts are 192.168.10.65 to 192.168.10.126. Router S0/0 is 192.1.2.109 and the ISP side is 192.1.2.110. Script results:
| Item | Result (script) |
| Public range 192.1.2.109 to 192.1.2.114 with a /29 mask | Not one subnet. .109 is in 192.1.2.104/29 and .114 is in 192.1.2.112/29. |
The book's first answer is fine:
Book answer 1 BOOK
access-list 1 permit 192.168.10.64 0.0.0.63
ip nat inside source list 1 pool Todd overload

It makes a one-address PAT pool using the router's own S0/0 address. The netmask can be replaced by prefix-length 29. Interfaces cannot use prefix-length. The ACL wildcard 0.0.0.63 matches the /26 block. BOOK
COMMON MISTAKE

The book's second answer is flawed. It suggests ip nat pool Todd 192.1.2.109 192.1.2.114 netmask 255.255.255.248. The script shows .109 and .114 are in two different /29 subnets, so the start and end do not fit one /29 mask. IOS checks that the pool range fits the mask. A secondary source says prefix-length makes sure all pool addresses are in the same subnet, so I expect IOS to reject it. UPDATED CHECK not run on hardware.
Also, .110 is the ISP's own address on the link, so it cannot be a public NAT address for you.

The book explains that extra addresses help with a "TCP-Reset issue" and a "NAK" when two hosts use the same source port. That explanation is muddled: TCP uses RST, not NAK, and PAT simply picks a different translated port for the second host. Extra pool addresses matter only when the ports of one address run out. UPDATED CHECK exact IOS behavior.
A cleaner solution for the same network uses the outside interface:
Alternative ADDED CHECK
access-list 1 permit 192.168.10.64 0.0.0.63
ip nat inside source list 1 interface Serial0/0 overload
interface FastEthernet0/0
ip nat inside
interface Serial0/0

| Topic | Remember |
| Purpose | NAT rewrites addresses so private hosts can use the Internet. It sits on the border router. Private ranges: 10/8, 172.16/12 (16 to 31), 192.168/16. |
| Other names | Network masquerading and IP masquerading are other names for NAT: rewriting the source or destination address of packets that pass through a router or firewall. BOOK |
| Three types | Static = one-to-one. Dynamic = pool, many-to-many. Overload (PAT) = many-to-one with ports. |
| Four names | Inside/outside = where the host is. Local = inside view. Global = outside view. Inside global = public address of the inside host. |
| Show column order | Pro, Inside global, Inside local, Outside local, Outside global. |

| Dynamic | ip nat pool NAME start end netmask\|prefix-length then ip nat inside source list N pool NAME |
| PAT | Add overload. One-line form: ip nat inside source list N interface TYPE NUM overload. |
| Pool rules | Case-sensitive name; right size; start and end inside one mask; no overlap with static addresses. |
| ACL | Selects traffic. No permit ip any any with NAT. |
| Verify | show ip nat translations, show ip nat statistics, debug ip nat (briefly), clear ip nat translation * (dynamic only). |

| Advantages | Saves public addresses; fixes overlap; flexible; no renumbering. |
| Disadvantages | Delay; loses end-to-end traceability; some apps break; complicates IPsec. |
| Order of operations | Inside to outside: route, then NAT. Outside to inside: NAT, then route. |

content.text: R1 CHECK
R1(config)# interface g0/0
R1(config-if)# ip nat inside
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# interface g0/1
R1(config-if)# ip nat outside

- ip nat inside / ip nat outside: mark which side is the LAN and which is the ISP. They do nothing until you add a NAT rule.
- ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 198.51.100.1: a default route that sends everything unknown to the ISP.
ISP CHECK
ISP(config)# interface g0/0
ISP(config-if)# no shutdown
ISP(config-if)# interface g0/1
ISP(config-if)# ip address 192.0.2.1 255.255.255.0
ISP(config-if)# no shutdown
ISP(config-if)# exit
- ip route 203.0.113.0 255.255.255.248 198.51.100.2: tells the ISP that your public block is behind R1. The ISP has no route to 192.168.10.0/24, as in real life.
Test: from PC1, ping 192.0.2.10. Expected result: it fails. The packet reaches NetSrv with a private source address, and the ISP has no route back. CHECK
R1 CHECK
R1(config)# ip nat inside source static 192.168.10.100 203.0.113.2
R1# show ip nat translations
- 192.168.10.100: inside local (SRV1). 203.0.113.2: inside global (the public address you chose).

Expected result: a line with --- ports: inside global 203.0.113.2, inside local 192.168.10.100. From NetSrv, ping 203.0.113.2 should be answered by SRV1, which shows static NAT works inbound too. From SRV1, ping 192.0.2.10 should work and add an icmp entry. CHECK

labs.title: Dynamic NAT with a two-address pool

content.text: R1 CHECK
R1(config)# access-list 1 permit 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.31
R1(config)# ip nat pool LABPOOL 203.0.113.3 203.0.113.4 netmask 255.255.255.248
R1(config)# ip nat inside source list 1 pool LABPOOL
R1# show ip nat translations
R1# show ip nat statistics
- access-list 1 permit 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.31: selects 192.168.10.0 to .31 (the three PCs). It selects traffic, it does not filter.
- ip nat pool LABPOOL ... netmask 255.255.255.248: two public addresses, no overlap with the static .2.
- ip nat inside source list 1 pool LABPOOL: no overload, so this is dynamic NAT.

Test: ping 192.0.2.10 from PC1, then PC2, then PC3. Expected result: PC1 and PC2 work and use .3 and .4. PC3 fails because the pool is used up. show ip nat statistics should show the pool with 2 addresses allocated. Run clear ip nat translation * and try PC3 again; it should now work. CHECK Entries last 24 hours by default, so the clear is needed.
R1, PAT with the outside interface CHECK
R1# clear ip nat translation *
R1(config)# no ip nat inside source list 1 pool LABPOOL
R1(config)# ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1 overload
R1# show ip nat translations

Test: ping NetSrv from all three PCs, then open http://192.0.2.10 in the PC web browsers. Expected result: all three work at the same time. Entries show inside global 198.51.100.2 with different port numbers, so this is PAT. CHECK
R1, PAT with a one-address pool CHECK
R1# clear ip nat translation *
R1(config)# no ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1 overload
R1(config)# ip nat pool PATPOOL 203.0.113.5 203.0.113.5 netmask 255.255.255.248
R1(config)# ip nat inside source list 1 pool PATPOOL overload
Expected result: the inside global address is now 203.0.113.5 with ports. This only works because the ISP routes 203.0.113.0/29 to R1. CHECK

content.text: Q1 In ip nat inside source static 10.1.1.1 170.46.2.2, which address is the inside local?
Answer: 10.1.1.1 - the first address is the private host, the second is the public address.
Q2 Name the two interface commands that must go with a NAT configuration.
Answer: ip nat inside and ip nat outside - NAT only translates between an inside and an outside interface.
Q3 Does a static NAT entry appear in the table before any traffic is sent?
Answer: Yes - it is configured, not created by traffic.
Q1 In dynamic NAT, what is the job of the access list?
Answer: To select which inside addresses are translated - it is not a security filter here.
Q2 Your config has ip nat pool Corp ... and ip nat inside source list 1 pool corp. Will it work?
Answer: No - pool names are case sensitive, so Corp and corp are different pools.
Q3 The pool has 2 addresses and no overload. Three inside hosts try to reach the Internet at the same time. What happens to the third?
Answer: It cannot be translated until a pool address is free - dynamic NAT without ports needs one public address per active host. CHECK exact symptom on hardware.
Q1 Which keyword changes dynamic NAT into PAT?
Answer: overload - it lets many hosts share one inside global address using ports.
Q2 Write the one-line PAT command that uses the outside interface Serial0/0/0 and ACL 1.
Answer: ip nat inside source list 1 interface Serial0/0/0 overload - the interface form needs no pool.
Q3 Besides the NAT command, what else must be configured for the line above to work?
Answer: A - CL 1, ip nat inside and ip nat outside on the interfaces - the ACL selects the hosts, the interface commands set the direction.
Q1 Which command shows the active NAT entries?
Answer: show ip nat translations - it is the translation table.
Q2 Which command shows hits, misses and expired translations?
Answer: show ip nat statistics - it is the NAT summary.
Q3 Does clear ip nat translation * remove static entries?
Answer: No, only dynamic entries - static entries are configured and stay. CHECK on hardware.
Q1 Which RFC defines the private IPv4 address ranges?
A. RFC 1918
B. RFC 2544
C. RFC 5737
D. RFC 791
Q2 Which address is NOT private?
Answer: C - the 172 private block ends at 172.31.255.255.
Q3 What is the public address of an inside host after translation called?
Answer: Inside global - inside host, seen from outside.
Q4 Which interface command marks the ISP-facing interface for NAT?
Answer: ip nat outside - it sets the direction.
Q5 Which keyword turns dynamic NAT into PAT?
Answer: overload - many hosts share one address using ports.
Q6 In ip nat inside source list 1 pool X, what does the ACL do?
Answer: It selects which inside addresses are translated - it is not a security filter.
Q7 True or false: a PAT entry in the table includes a port number.
Answer: True - that is how hosts are told apart.
Q8 Give the column order of show ip nat translations.
Answer: Pro, Inside global, Inside local, Outside local, Outside global - global first, local second.
Q9 A dynamic pool has 2 addresses and no overload. Three hosts try to go out at once. What happens to the third?
Answer: It cannot be translated until a pool address is free - one public address per active host. CHECK symptom on hardware.
Q10 What is the ACL wildcard for 192.168.10.64/26?
Answer: 0.0.0.63 - block size 64, so wildcard is 63 (checked by script).
Q11 Which mask fits the pool 203.0.113.1 to 203.0.113.6?
Answer: 255.255.255.248 (/29) - 203.0.113.0/29 has usable hosts .1 to .6 (checked by script).
Q12 How many addresses are in ip nat pool P 203.0.113.9 203.0.113.10 netmask 255.255.255.252?
Answer: 2 - a /30 has two usable hosts, .9 and .10 (checked by script).
Q13 Why might you use ip nat inside source list 1 interface g0/1 overload instead of a pool?
Answer: No pool to edit, and it follows the interface address if the ISP changes it - good for a single public address.
Q14 Which command clears all dynamic entries? Does it remove static ones?
Answer: C - clear ip nat translation *. No, static entries stay - static entries are configured. CHECK on hardware.
Q15 What are the default timeouts for simple entries and for UDP port entries?
Answer: 86,400 s (24 h) and 300 s (5 min) - values from Cisco community and secondary sources. CHECK on your platform.
Q16 Why is routing a common cause of NAT problems?
Answer: The packet still has to be routed before or after translation - Cisco's order: route then NAT outbound, NAT then route inbound.
Q17 NAT is configured but nothing translates and the statistics show no hits. What do you check first?
Answer: The inside and outside interface commands, then the ACL - the book says wrong inside/outside is a very common error.
Q18 You need fixed public addresses for 5 servers. Which NAT type and how many public addresses?
Answer: Static NAT, 5 addresses - one-to-one.
Q19 Which type is typical for a home with one public IP?
Answer: PAT (overload) - many-to-one.
Q20 What lets PAT tell inside hosts apart?
Answer: The source port number - the same inside global IP is shared.
Q21 In normal web browsing, how do outside local and outside global compare?
Answer: They are the same address - the destination is not translated.
Q22 Is NAT a security feature?
Answer: No - it hides addresses as a side effect. Use ACLs or a firewall. ADDED General knowledge.
Q23 Which v2.0 exam objective covers this chapter?
Answer: 4.3 Configure NAT/PAT on IOS XE routers - read from Cisco's v2.0 outline.
Q24 Your pool is Corp and the rule says pool corp. Does it work?
Answer: No - pool names are case sensitive.
Q25 A packet arrives on the outside interface for an inside host. What is the order: route then NAT, or NAT then route?
Answer: NAT, then route - Cisco's order for outside-to-inside traffic.
Q26 Why should you not use 198.18.0.0/15 as your public range in a lab?
Answer: It is benchmarking space, not publicly reachable. Use RFC 5737 ranges - IANA special-purpose registry.
